corr.head: StressTyp2's coding matches the source only in part
corr.detail: StressTyp2 entry: "Jaru; Djaru: primary stress on the left-most heavy syllable, else on the initial syllable; no secondary stress". The source gives: Stress generally on the first syllable of the word; a long vowel /aa/ generally takes the stress even when non-initial ([baláːɳ], rarely [bálaːɳ]; [ketaŋáːɳiɲ]). Stress is phonetic only, non-distinctive. — StressTyp2's 'left-most heavy syllable, else initial' (F/F, heavy = long vowels) captures the gist, but Tsunoda states both clauses only as tendencies ('generally', with a 'rarely' initial-stress variant), never discusses words with more than one long vowel, calls stress non-distinctive, and adds a morpheme-conditioned (CVC/trisyllabic)…

ev.cite: Tsunoda, Tasaku. 1981. The Djaru Language of Kimberley, Western Australia. Pacific Linguistics B-78. Canberra: Australian National University. — section 2.7 'Stress and Pitch', pp.47-48
ev.text: Phonetically, both stress and pitch occur but they are 'phonologically irrelevant or nondistinctive' (Trubetzkoy 1969:31) in Djaru; they do not differentiate meanings of words (as the English stress or Japanese pitch). 660.dq: STRESS generally falls on the first syllable of a word ... A long vowel /aa/ [a:] generally takes a stress even if it is not word-initial.
660.heavy: Only the long vowel /aa/ [a:] is said to attract stress ('generally takes a stress even if it is not word-initial'); separately, a disyllabic second morpheme 'containing a CVC syllable' (or any trisyllabic+ morpheme) may carry its own (often more prominent) stress — CVC figures only in that morpheme-level condition, not as a general syllable-weight criterion.
660.dflt: initial syllable of the word (and optionally of a qualifying second morpheme)
660.prule: Stress generally on the first syllable of the word; a long vowel /aa/ generally takes the stress even when non-initial ([baláːɳ], rarely [bálaːɳ]; [ketaŋáːɳiɲ]). Stress is phonetic only, non-distinctive.
660.srule: No secondary or rhythmic stress described within simple words (one stress marked: máŋari, [bálawaɳ]); Tsunoda draws no primary/secondary distinction. A second stress arises only by morphology: in compounds, reduplications and words with derivational suffixes the first syllable of the second morpheme can also be stressed if that morpheme is trisyllabic or longer, or disyllabic containing a CVC syllable, and it is then more often the more prominent one (búlu-ḍuwal ~ búlu-ḍúwal ~ bulu-ḍúwal).

evidence_works.work: Senge 2015, A Grammar of Wanyjirra, a language of Northern Australia (PhD thesis, Australian National University: pp.67, 75, 101-102)
evidence_works.detail: Section 2.7 'Stress' (printed p.101): 'Stress in Wanyjirra is characterised as increased loudness, and sometimes, length although it is not phonologically contrastive. Primary stress falls on the first syllable of the phonological word. If the word contains more than three syllables, secondary stress generally occurs on the penultimate syllable.' (2-86 d ˈwarndaˌrdurru, e ˈwayiˌwarrang). 'However, if a polysyllabic word consists of a stem and a disyllabic or longer suffix, or if it involves compounding or reduplication processes, the first syllables of the second morphemes (i.e., suffixes, compounding morphemes or reduplicated morphemes) receive a stress.' (2-88 ˈngarlu-ˌyarung, ˈgilagi-ˌwunyja, ˈWanyjirra-ˌjaru-wu, ˈwarnang-ˌwarnang). Printed p.102: 'A long vowel /aː/ in non-initial syllables also tends to receive secondary stress even if the word is not polysyllabic as in (2-89).' (2-89 ʹbaˌlaarn 'turtle', ʹwarnˌdaarraj 'in a line'); 'In fossilised reduplicates, primary stress is found on the initial syllable of the word and secondary stress may optionally appear on the initial syllable of the second repeated segments.' (2-90 ʹgarrajˌgarraj ~ ʹgarrajgarraj). Section 2.2.3.3 (printed p.67) states the long-vowel clause differently: 'the long vowel /aː/ receives a stress wherever it occurs in a word. Stress is usually placed on the first syllable of the word if the word does not contain the long vowel (§2.7).' Section 2.3.2.4 (printed p.75) transcribes balaarn as [ʹpɐlɐːɳ] with initial primary stress. Agrees with the entry on initial primary stress, non-contrastive stress and a stress on the first syllable of a second morpheme in suffixed, compound and reduplicated words; adds a penultimate secondary stress in words of more than three syllables (absent from Tsunoda); on the same lexeme balaarn 'turtle' it marks primary-initial with secondary on the long vowel where Tsunoda gives Djaru [baláːɳ] (rarely [bálaːɳ]).
evidence_works.variety: Wanyjirra, which Senge treats as a distinct variety in the Ngumpin dialect chain ('often treated as a dialect of Jaru or Gurindji', p.7), not the Djaru (Wawarl/Nyininy) of Tsunoda 1981 that the entry's identity field names.

The catalog has no Wanyjirra record; its Jaru [jaru1254] bibliography already lists Senge 2015's Wanyjirra grammar as a sister variety, so the row is placed there and does not bear on the Djaru long-vowel clause.

contra.head: The published descriptions contradict each other
contra.detail: Primaries irreconcilable: Ras 1982/1985 = weak penult stress with schwa-conditioned shift to final (a vowel-quality QS rule, the basis of StressTyp2's P/U and WALS 15A right-edge coding); Poedjosoedarmo 1982:49 = final; Horne 1961:26 = no fixed position; Stoel 2006 (instrumental AM analysis, Banyumas dialect) and Goedemans & van Zanten 2007 (Javanese-substrate Indonesian: no acoustic stress correlates, penult/final accent equally acceptable) = no word stress, phrasal boundary tones whose H aligns penult-or-final with a schwa-penult favouring final alignment -- i.e. the 'schwa rule' survives only as a tendency in boundary-tone alignment.

661.dq: Stoel 2006 abstract: "As Javanese is a language without lexical stress, there are no pitch accents. Boundary tones are associated with the Accentual Phrase (AP)." (contrast Ras 1985 via StressTyp2, which describes a word accent distinct from an optional phrase-level 'affective accent' realised by final lengthening).
661.dloc: Stoel 2006: p.1, sec. 3 'Stress' (+ abstract, sec. 5.1); Goedemans & van Zanten 2007: p.41; Ras 1985
661.heavy: Ras (1982/1985): a penult whose vowel is schwa /ə/ rejects stress (stress goes to the final); i.e. full (non-schwa) vowel = stressable, schwa = light. StressTyp2 note: ': full vowels'. No role for vowel length or codas is stated.
661.dflt: final (Ras: stress on the final 'even when this syllable also contains /@/')
661.prule: Ras 1985 (carried): penultimate stress; if the penult vowel is /ə/, final stress (even if the final also has /ə/). Poedjosoedarmo 1982: final stress. Horne 1961:26: no fixed stress position ('it does not matter which syllable... gets the loudest stress'). Stoel 2006: no lexical stress; phrase-boundary tones (H of HL%) align with penult or final, penult-schwa favouring final alignment.
661.srule: Not mentioned in Stoel 2006 (whole paper, sec. 3-5) or Goedemans & van Zanten 2007:39-55: both analyse Javanese as having no word stress ('there are no stressed syllables'), so no word-level secondary stress arises. Legacy claim only: Ras 1985 (via StressTyp2 entry, carried) reports that when two or more suffixes move the main stress to the new penult 'a secondary stress [is left] on the fourth syllable from the right' (the root's former stress site); no rhythmic secondary stress; StressTyp2's own code is 'Secondary: None'.

Horne [4], on the other hand, denies that there are any fixed rules for stress in Javanese, and claims that any syllable can get the main stress. 661.loc: Stoel 2006: p.1, sec. 3 'Stress' (+ abstract, sec. 5.1); Goedemans & van Zanten 2007: p.41; Ras 1985 via StressTyp2 entry (no page).
661.idn: Stoel 2006, the deciding instrumental source, describes the Banyumas dialect of Javanese from a single speaker; Goedemans & van Zanten 2007 measured Indonesian as spoken by a Javanese speaker from Klaten, not Javanese itself. Ras 1985, Poedjosoedarmo 1982 and Horne 1961…
661.exq_: I assume that not only Indonesian as spoken by speakers of Javanese does not have stress, but that this is also the case for Javanese itself. As there are no stressed syllables, there are also no pitch accents, and I will therefore use only boundary tones in my description.

morph.src: Main source: Suharno, Ignatius. 1982. A Descriptive Study of Javanese. Pacific Linguistics D-45. Canberra: ANU (ch. 2 'The structure of the word', ch. 3 'The structure of the sentence'). Tokens and cross-checks: Vander Klok, Jozina. 2012. Tense, aspect, and modal markers in Paciran Javanese. PhD dissertation, McGill University (ch. 1 sec. 7.2 'Verbal morphology in Paciran Javanese', sec. 8 examples). Stress facts: Stoel, Ruben. 2006. The intonation of Banyumas Javanese. Speech Prosody 2006, sec. 2-3 (a copy), with Goedemans & van Zanten 2007:41 (in the copy consulted) for the Ras/Poedjosoedarmo/Horne statements.
morph.rootq: Neither morphology source has a word-stress section: Suharno 1982 only remarks, on Ce-reduplication, that 'the vowel of the first syllable of the verb so reduplicated ... being unstressed, is always E' (p.24), and 'There is no way of saying in which syllable of a non-monosyllabic word its meaning is centered' (p.16); Vander Klok 2012 says nothing about stress. The stress source of record (Stoel 2006 sec. 3, on disk) states the rules over the WORD, not the root: 'There is no agreement among authors on the stress pattern of Javanese. Poedjosoedarmo [9] claims that Javanese has final stress, while Ras [10] states that stress falls on the penultimate syllable, but if it contains a schwa, then…
morph.elicq: Stoel 2006 sec. 2 'Materials': 'The present study is based on a small corpus, that was produced by Maria Ulfah, a native speaker of the Banyumas dialect of Javanese. The corpus contains about 350 question-answer pairs and a short story. ... The sentence pairs were shown one-by-one to the speaker, who was asked to memorize them, and then pronounce them without being able to see the text. The short story was composed on the spot by the speaker.' (analysed with pitch tracks, Figures 1-4; sec. 5.1: 'In all the examples in the corpus, the H target of a non-final HL% tone is aligned with the penultimate syllable, except if it contains a schwa'). The older rule statements it cites…
morph.stmt: Javanese is mildly agglutinative with a mixed profile: voice and agent-person marking are prefixal (actor-voice homorganic nasal (a)N-, passive di-/ka- ~ kE-, agent taq- 'by me', k6q- 'by you', plus literary infixes -in-, -um-), while applicative/causative (-i, -ake/-no), imperative (-En, -6/-a), nominalising -an, definite -(n)e and possessive -ku/-mu are suffixal, plural and reciprocal use reduplication, and tense-aspect, modality, negation and interrogation are free preverbal words; in Suharno's inventory (1982:18-19) 'The affixes that are related to a verb are... The prefixes: 1. m6r6-... 11. k6q-; The infixes: 12. -in-, 13. -um-, 14. -r-; The suffixes: 15. -(n)i, 16. -an, 17. -En…

662.dq: The stress in Woisika is free. Its place is unpredictable in basic words (i.e. non-composed words without affixes) which consist of two or more syllables. ... [4.2] Minimal accentual units are the basic entities, the building blocks, in the prominence organisation of the utterance. They can be words or longer stretches and they are combined with other monosyllabic or polysyllabic words so as to f…
662.heavy: none: the source states no syllable-weight criterion for stress; stress placement is described as free/distinctive (examples of initial, final and penultimate stress include open and closed syllables alike, e.g. /'sibe/ 'chicken', /ta'pul/ 'crab', /si'lota/ 'to stretch').
662.prule: Stress is culminative and free: its place within the minimal accentual unit is distinctive and unpredictable in basic (unaffixed, non-compound) words of two or more syllables; initial, final and penultimate stress all occur (minimal pairs /'sapatu/ 'Saturday' vs /sa'patu/ 'shoe'); final stress in words of 3+ syllables is very sporadic; certain prefixes (personal prefixes of one series and /mi/) always attract stress; accentual doublets occur.
662.srule: None at word level: stress is culminative, with 'one and only one' prominence peak per minimal accentual unit (a polysyllabic word alone is such a unit; words of five-six syllables carry a single stress mark); secondary or rhythmic stress is not mentioned anywhere in ch. 4 (pp. 86-93).
662.quote: A satisfactory treatment of stress and intonation phenomena in Woisika awaits further study. ... Stress in Woisika is culminative; a syllable carrying the stress is more prominent as compared to its contiguous syllables. It operates in minimal accentual units (m.a.u.), i.e. "a string of syllables of which one and only one at a time [...] carries a prominence peak" (Ebeling 1968:138). A grammatically independent form may or may not coincide with a minimal accentual unit ... Other examples are: ... /'sapatu/ 'Saturday' vs. /sa'patu/ 'shoe' /'sija/ 'our stool' vs. /si'ja/ 'we go' These examples …
662.idn: Stokhof's 'Woisika' is Glottolog's Kamang (kama1365), central Alor; of the ten provisional variants he lists (Lembur, Petimpui, Kamana, Kamot, Kamengmi, Ateita, Pido, Langkuru/Kolomana, Silaipui, Apui) the description is based on the Ateita variant (informants from Manegeng, Susimang, Maumang, Puiwela; sec. 5.1 p. 94).

corr.detail: StressTyp2 entry: "Kara: primary stress on the right-most heavy syllable, else on the initial syllable; secondary stress: Rhythm (v14)". 663.dq: Stress is determined by three factors: vowel quality, syllable closure, and position in the word. ... an ordered system of rules governing stress placement in all words of two syllables or more.
663.dloc: section 2.3 Stress, pp.108-110 (quoted passage pp.108-109 = SIL scan (Internet Archive copy) pp.10-11, p.110, exceptions and secondary stress = archive.org, p.12); Kara OPD p.3 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)'
663.heavy: Two-tier scale: (1) a syllable with a nucleus of /a/ (vowel quality; 'the most important factor'), over (2) a closed syllable ('a final closed syllable takes precedence over a nonfinal one'); open non-/a/ syllables are light. No vowel-length criterion. OPD p.3: "Syllables with the phoneme /ɑ/, and closed syllables are 'heavy' and normally stressed."
663.prule: Primary stress on the last syllable with an /a/ nucleus; if none, on a closed syllable (a final closed syllable takes precedence over a nonfinal one); if neither, on the stem-initial syllable. Prefixal syllables (incl. reduplicative prefixes) are almost never stressed. Each step is hedged ('almost always', 'normally', 'generally').
663.srule: p.110: 'Primary and secondary stress may not occur on contiguous syllables. Thus, in two syllable words there is no secondary stress. Similarly, in three syllable words with stress on the second syllable there is no secondary stress. If primary stress falls on the initial syllable, secondary stress falls on the ultimate syllable in three syllable words and on the penultimate in words of greater than three syllables, as shown in (44l). If the second syllable is stressed in a four syllable word, the ultimate syllable receives secondary stress. If primary stress falls on the third syllable or later, secondary stress falls on the initial syllable (unless it is a prefix in which case it will fall on the second syllable).' Secondary placement is positional (quantity-insensitive) given the primary; examples 42-45 show it (e.g. [ˌɣə.lə.'pʰʊŋ], ['pʰi.sə.ˌne], ['mə.tʰə.ɸe.ˌtʰə.mə], [pʰe.'bo.gə.ˌne]). OPD 2004 p.3 restates the initial-primary case.

663.sec_rule: Two stress levels; secondary stress is realised mainly as changing pitch. With the default initial primary stress, secondary stress falls on the final syllable in three-syllable words and on the penult in words of four or more syllables (Schlie OPD p.3); the 1993 transcriptions (p.109) also mark an initial secondary stress when a heavy syllable carries primary stress on the third or a later syllable (e.g. [ˌɣə.lə.ˈpʰʊŋ], [ˌŋu.ru.βə.ˈpɔŋ]). Positional, quantity-insensitive.
663.sec_quote: ... secondary stress of changing pitch. Primary stress normally occurs on the initial syllable with secondary stress on the ultimate syllable in three syllable words and on the penultimate in words longer than three syllables. In two syllable words, the first syllable is normally stressed. Exceptions to these rules occur when a 'heavy' syllable draws the stress to itself.

tn.quote: Based on our data, the system can be stated relatively simply: contrast in pitch (/H/ v /L/) is only possible on accented syllables. Otherwise, unstressed syllables are always low in pitch. ... our pilot study confirms the existence of contrastive tone in Kara. ... At this stage, we are certain that Kara has two tonemes (high and low), based on minimal pairs we have been able to find, as well as on native speaker intuitions and our own auditory, and acoustic analysis. There is some evidence of mid tone, but it appears to be a predictable variant of L before final glottal stops in our corpus.
tn.cite: Hajek, John & Mary Stevens (2004). Tonal activity in Kara, an Austronesian language spoken in New Britain [sic]. In Cassidy, Cox, Mannell & Palethorpe (eds), Proceedings of the 10th Australian International Conference on Speech Science and Technology, Sydney: ASSTA, 295-300.
tn.locator: p.300, end of section 5 'Discussion' and section 6 'Conclusion'
tn.note: Two level tonemes H vs L, contrast only on the accented syllable; unstressed syllables low; mid = variant of L before final glottal stop. Schlie & Schlie 1993 fn.4: tone 'does not seem to be a factor'

corr.detail: StressTyp2 entry: "Karok: primary stress on the left-most heavy syllable, else on the final syllable; no information on secondary stress". The source gives: Pitch-accent system (Bright: three accent phonemes acute/circumflex/none, at most one accented syllable per word; Sandy/Macaulay: privative H tone lexically specified or assigned by morphology). Stress is parasitic on tone: it falls on the syllable bearing the H (right edge of H span). Only where no H is present does a weight default apply: lexically unaccented words get stress on a long vowel if present, else final (Bright 1957:13; Sandy attributes the final H to an Accentual-Phrase boundary tone, absent utterance-finally).

664.heavy: long vowels: Bright 'a long voweled syllable' attracts default stress in unaccented words; Sandy: placement 'sensitive to the presence of long vowels' (H on the syllable before the rightmost long vowel), plus avoidance of H on a short vowel in a closed syllable (*(C)V́C) in roots; codas do not count as heavy.

664.prule: Pitch-accent system (Bright: three accent phonemes acute/circumflex/none, at most one accented syllable per word; Sandy/Macaulay: privative H tone lexically specified or assigned by morphology). Stress is parasitic on tone: it falls on the syllable bearing the H (right edge of H span). Only where no H is present does a weight default apply: lexically unaccented words get stress on a long vowel if present, else final (Bright 1957:13; Sandy attributes the final H to an Accentual-Phrase boundary tone, absent utterance-finally). In derived/inflected words Sandy's 'basic derived accentuation' puts H+stress on the syllable immediately before the rightmost long vowel, else on the penult, unless blocked by a protected (lexical or derived) HL structure or stem-final accent morphology.
664.srule: None: 'Karuk stress is culminative and obligatory, with one stress per word' (Sandy 2017:19); 'Each accented word bears exactly one stress' (p.42). Possible phonetic secondary stress (alternating intensity/vowel duration in longer words, p.20; lesser consonant length, p.21) is flagged by the author as unconfirmed, pending phonetic study (sec. 9.2 p.196).

664.tone: Sparse-tone / pitch-accent system: at most one privative H tone per word (accentual phrase), lexically specified on roots or assigned/erased by morphology; surface contrast H vs HL (falling) on long vowels, H only on short vowels; stress falls on the syllable containing the H-bearing mora, so stress location is predictable from tone but not conversely; lexically unaccented words get a phrase-final H% (toneless utterance-finally).

tn.quote: Das Slovinzische unterscheidet zwei qualitativ verschiedene Akzente, den scharfen Ton und den dehnenden Ton. Der scharfe Ton ist in exspiratorischer Beziehung ein eingipfliger, einfach fallender, schwach geschnittener Akzent. In musikalischer Beziehung ist derselbe ebenfalls fallend. ... Der dehnende Ton ist ein exspiratorisch zweigipfliger Akzent mit stärkerem ersten Gipfel. ... der zweite Gipfel tonisch höher liegt als der erste. ... Der scharfe Ton findet sich nur bei den Langstufenvokalen ... Der dehnende Ton findet sich nur bei den Kurzstufenvokalen
tn.translation: Slovincian distinguishes two qualitatively different accents, the sharp tone and the extending (drawling) tone. The sharp tone is, expiratorily, a single-peaked, simply falling, weakly cut accent. Musically it is likewise falling. ... The extending tone is an expiratorily two-peaked accent with a stronger first peak. ... the second peak lies tonally higher than the first. ... The sharp tone is found only with the long-grade vowels ... The extending tone is found only with the short-grade vowels
tn.cite: Lorentz, Friedrich. 1903. Slovinzische Grammatik. St. Petersburg: Kaiserliche Akademie der Wissenschaften.

tn.note: Two accent qualities on the stressed syllable: sharp (falling) on long-grade vowels, extending (two-peaked, 2nd peak higher) on short-grade ones; өu̯ from ъl/ьl differs by accent quality alone (§48).

morph.rootq: Koul & Wali 2006 §2.2.2 (p.16), the entire stress section: 'Stress is not a distinctive feature. However, since Kashmiri is a syllable-timed language, sometimes, individual words are stressed for emphasis.' No reference to root, stem or affixes. (The weight-based description in Morén 2000, restating Bhatt 1989, is likewise purely phonological: 'main stress in Kashmiri is as far left in a word as possible. However, it is weight sensitive, and retracts to the left-most heaviest syllable of the word (excluding final syllables)' (ROA-273 p.6); its only morphological remark is 'in monomorphemic disyllabic words, the final syllable is never stressed' (p.5).)
morph.elicq: Koul & Wali 2006 give no evidential basis for the two-sentence stress statement (§2.2.2 p.16, quoted above). Morén 2000: 'All data are taken from Bhatt (1989).' (ROA-273 p.4) — an unpublished ms.; the examples are isolated citation forms ([phí.ki.ri], [ni.rán.jan]) but no elicitation method is stated.
morph.stmt: Koul & Wali (p.24-25): 'Kashmiri is a mix of both the agglutinating and inflectional type. It shows both types of morphemic processes across most lexical categories such as nouns, verbs, and adjectives'; all inflection and derivation they describe is suffixal or stem-internal (ablaut, final-consonant palatalization) — e.g. 'Plurals are formed from singular forms by suffixation, palatalization, and vowel changes' (p.28), 'The pronominal suffixes always follow the basic gender-number suffixes' (p.83) — and no prefix appears anywhere in the grammar (the only preverbal grammatical markers are the free prohibitive particle mɨ/mat and the optional question particle k'a:).

666.cfw: The two dedicated studies of Kashmiri stress, Bhatt 1989 as reported in Morén 2000 and the first-hand Srinagar study of Munshi & Crowhurst 2012, agree that stress is weight-sensitive and falls on the leftmost heaviest non-final syllable, while the only contrary placement, Kelkar 1984's one-line remark of automatic light initial stress (from Kelkar & Trisal 1964), comes from a 1960s sketch that leaves prosody for future study and coincides with the default case, and Kachru 1973, Bhat 1987, Koul 2005 and Koul & Wali 2006 say only that stress is non-contrastive and used for emphasis without giving any placement.

667.dq: The preceding examples represent single words that take stress as independent constituents. But very often, two or more words are grouped together with a single footing that determines the location of stress for the entire phrase (Buckley & Gluckman 2012).
667.dloc: Buckley 2013/2014 sec. 1 'Kashaya stress', pp. 1-2 (exx. 1-7); Buckley 2018 slides 4-5, 8
667.heavy: heavy = closed syllable (CVC) or long vowel; both form nonbranching iambic feet; a leftmost (CV:) foot additionally triggers accent shift to the following foot (foot extrametricality); stressed open CV undergoes iambic lengthening
667.dflt: third syllable (second when extrametricality is blocked), with iambic lengthening of the stressed open syllable
667.prule: Iambs left to right; first syllable extrametrical unless the root is monosyllabic and unprefixed; main stress on the leftmost foot: 2nd syllable if heavy, else 3rd (1st if heavy else 2nd without extrametricality); a leftmost (CV:) foot, even if later shortened, passes the accent to the next foot: 3rd if heavy else 4th; (CV:)+CV surfacing as (CVCV:) (Foot Flipping) sends it to the next foot: 4th if heavy else 5th.
667.srule: None: 'there is not clear evidence of secondary phonetic prominences beyond the main stress, so only the pitch accent is transcribed' (Buckley 2021:10); 'There are no secondary stresses in the language' (Buckley 1997:10). Iterative iambic feet are inferred from iambic lengthening only, not from audible secondary stresses.
667.quote: Kashaya, a Pomoan language of northern California, has a complex but almost entirely regular system for assigning stress (Oswalt 1961, 1988). The basic analysis involves iambic feet beginning at the left edge, with iambic lengthening of stressed open syllables (Buckley 1994a,b); however, vowels located in a large class of “outer” suffixes, such as -mela below, do not undergo lengthening. Main stress falls on the first foot; secondary stress is not transcribed in the sources, but iterative feet are required to account for iambic lengthening and other phenomena. In words with a monosyllabic roo…

667.idn: Kashaya, a Pomoan language of northern California (no dialect named); data: Examples are drawn from Oswalt (1964) and his unpublished dictionary and field notes, housed in the California Language Archive at the University of California, Berkeley…

tn.quote: The leftmost foot is normally the location of primary stress, defined here as an abstract metrical prominence that correlates with the foot head. The main cue for this prominence is a pitch accent, i.e. a raised F0. Although iterative metrical feet are well motivated by the location of lengthened vowels, there is not clear evidence of secondary phonetic prominences beyond the main stress, so only the pitch accent is transcribed. If the leftmost foot is nonbranching /CV:/, accent is shifted to the following foot.

tn.note: Metrical primary stress cued by a pitch accent (raised F0) on the head of the leftmost foot of an accent phrase; no tone inventory; short phrases may go unaccented. 2014 paper is silent on pitch.

668.srule: Secondary stress differs from primary only in lower intensity. When several non-adjacent syllables bear the emic high-mid falling tone, main stress is on the last of them and every other HM-falling syllable carries secondary stress (rule c); an affixed (extended) phonological word carries up to four secondary-stressed syllables, main stress on the last stressed syllable, the earlier stressed syllables (lexical on high-tone morphemes) being secondary. No alternating or counting rule is given.

668.tone: Kaure is tonal: two emic tones, high level /1/ and high-mid falling /12/, with many monosyllabic minimal pairs (sec. 3.4.1); both surface as such only on stressed syllables and are lowered on unstressed ones (Rules 1-5, sec. 3.4.2). Stress is realised as intensity and tone; an emic high-mid falling tone attracts stress, while among high-level-tone syllables stress placement is phonemic (sec. 3.2).

morph.stmt: 'The Kaure verb consists of a central root word, which can be both prefixed and suffixed. Prefixes indicate the number of the subject, or the imperative. Suffixes mark tense, negative vs. positive, desire, distance, and question vs. statement vs. command.' 670.srule: Non-primary stresses are the heads of trochaic disyllabic feet (Round 2009). Lexically, feet align with the left edge of every root, with the right edge of nominal roots of four or more syllables (verbal roots align differently), with underlyingly stressed suffixes, and with each member of a compound; post-lexically, further disyllabic trochees are built as far to the left as possible so that no two adjacent syllables are left unfooted. Stress clash never surfaces; there is no syllable weight and long vowels do not attract stress. Root+termination words: 2 syll 10, 3 syll 100, 4 syll 1010, 5 syll 10100 (10010 on a five-syllable root), 6 syll 100100.

671.dflt: penult in 2-3-syllable words (= initial in disyllables) per Abdel-Hafiz 1988:21; initial per Armbruster 1960:95 (carried; Hayes 1980:112 groups Dongolese Nubian with Classical Arabic 'rightmost non-final heavy, otherwise initial')
671.prule: Kenzi (Abdel-Hafiz 1988:21-22): stress is non-phonemic and regular; monosyllables stressed; in 2- and 3-syllable words stress falls on the penult unless there is a long vowel, in which case the long syllable is stressed (examples show final long-vowel syllables taking stress: gillí:t, iccí:n); a few bisyllables are lexically marked for final stress. Dongolawi (Armbruster 1960:95 via StressTyp2, carried): all-light words have initial stress; a heavy syllable (CVV, non-final CVC, final CVVC) takes stress; with several heavies the rightmost is stressed.
671.srule: Not mentioned in Abdel-Hafiz 1988, sect. 2.3 'Stress', pp. 21-22 (Kenzi; the rule is stated for words of one to three syllables and every example carries a single stress mark).
671.quote: 2.3 Stress. In KN stress is not phonemic; it does not show semantic contrast. All words are regularly stressed as follows: the stress falls on the first syllable of one-syllable words: One-syllable words jóm 'hit' íd 'man' nóg 'go'. With two- and three-syllable words, (unless there is a long vowel) the stress falls on the penultimate. two-syllable words: dógir 'devil' jágin 'push' térig 'deaf' gútti 'kick'; three-syllable words: kašránge 'a plant' jagá:de 'wet' kilílle 'cry of joy' kanísse 'dough'. [p.22] A long syllable is always stressed: gillí:t 'organ' kerrí:t 'yogurt' iccí:n 'scorpion'. …
671.idn: primary source (Abdel-Hafiz 1988) describes Kunuz Nubian (KN), i.e. the Kenzi/Kenuzi (Mattokki) half of Kenuzi-Dongola (Glottolog dialect kenu1243, ISO xnz), 'spoken in New Nubia, near Kom Ombo in Southern Egypt'; the Dongolawi/Andaandi half (dong1288, ISO dgl) rests only on Armbruster 1960:95 as paraphrased by…
671.exq_: There are a few bisyllabic words that are stressed on the final syllable rather than the penultimate as predicted; such words are marked for stress in the lexicon: affí 'boy' kofré 'a plant' uffé 'blow'

morph.elicq: No method statement specific to stress; the section's evidence is lists of isolated citation forms ('One-syllable words: jom hit, id man, nog go ... two-syllable words / three-syllable words: dogir devil ... kaSrange a plant ...', §2.3 p.21), and the data statement is introspective: 'Both my wife and myself are native speakers of KN; we were raised in the same province. I, therefore, heavily relied on our speech for most of the data.' (§1.2 Data, p.10). No frame sentences, texts or measurements are mentioned for stress; the glossed texts in Appendix 1 carry no stress marks.
morph.stmt: Predominantly suffixing: 'The morphosyntactic processes used in KN verbs are mainly two: suffixation and compounding. Suffixation is the most predominant process. Prefixation is only used inflectionally: the Progressive a- and Future Tense bi-.' (§3.20 p.104); in the noun, Number, Case and (In)definiteness are all suffixes ('Case and Definiteness... morphemes are suffixed to the last element of a noun phrase', §3.1 p.71; 'Case marking is expressed by suffixes for all cases except the nominative which is unmarked', Conclusion p.280), the only nominal prefixes being the kinship possessor prefixes an-/in-/tin- on nine dependent kin roots (§3.113 p.82).

672.dq: Kera has no obvious word-level phonetic stress ... In Kera, words do not generally exhibit a pattern where exactly one syllable is more intense than the others, so we cannot claim that intensity is used as a word accent. However, intensity is used at the level of the foot ... Even at phrase level, there appears to be very little use of intensity unless a word is being particularly stressed for em…
672.dloc: Pearce 2006: abstract p.259; p.260; (2)-(3) pp.262-263; p.264; p.269. Ebert 1979:58 (StressTyp2 entry, carried).
672.heavy: Heavy = (C)VV (lexically long or lengthened vowel) and (C)VC; light = (C)V (Pearce 2006:262). Ebert 1979:58 (carried) instead ranks long vowels, then high tone.
672.dflt: Pearce: does not arise - /CVCV/ is repaired to (CVC) phrase-medially or (CV.CVV) phrase-finally so every foot has a heavy head. Ebert 1979 (carried): first high-toned syllable, else final syllable (excluding nominal -i / schwa).
672.prule: Pearce 2006: no word-level stress / no word-level metrical head; words are parsed into quantity-sensitive iambic feet (heavy (CVV)/(CVC) or light-heavy (CV.CVV)/(CV.CVC)), every foot head obligatorily heavy and cued by duration, intensity and [-ATR] allophones; heads of multiple feet are equally prominent; a stray light CV may stand unfooted at the right edge phrase-finally. Ebert 1979:58 (carried via StressTyp2): 'A syllable with a long vowel is stressed. If there are no long vowels the first syllable with a high tone is stressed... If a word does not have long vowels or high tones, stress is on the final syllable as long as it is not the nominal ending -i or schwa.'
672.srule: None: 'Kera has no word-level stress' (p.259); 'words do not generally exhibit a pattern where exactly one syllable is more intense than the others, so we cannot claim that intensity is used as a word accent. However, intensity is used at the level of the foot... Words with two feet have roughly the same intensity for the heads of both feet' (p.269) - no primary or secondary word stress; equal foot-level prominence on the head (always heavy) of every iambic foot.

[p.260] Kera has no obvious word-level phonetic stress, but we will see that there is clearly an active metrical structure which interacts with the tonal system. ... it presents a language in which the association of tones makes reference to within-word metrical structure, while there is no evidence of a word-level metrical head. ... [pp.262-263] (2)…

672.idn: Kera, 'the standard Kera dialect' (main Kera-speaking area south of Fianga); data: Speakers from south of Fianga, Southern Chad; recordings made in Chad January-March 2004, with field notes from 1992-2002
672.exq_: In Kera, words do not generally exhibit a pattern where exactly one syllable is more intense than the others, so we cannot claim that intensity is used as a word accent. However, intensity is used at the level of the foot: intensity is greater for the head of the foot.
672.tone: Tone language: three underlying tones (H, M, L), enhanced by VOT differences; no contour tones. Tone association refers to iambic foot structure (TBU = the foot in words of three or more syllables, the syllable in shorter words), but there is no word-level stress or metrical head; foot heads are cued by duration, intensity and vowel allophony (Pearce 2006: 259-260, 272-274).

morph.rootq: Pearce 2006 (abstract): 'Kera has no word-level stress, but the heads of its quantity-sensitive iambic feet are cued by duration, intensity and vowel allophony'. Pearce 2007 thesis section 2.2.10 (p.68): 'Note however that the heavy syllable can be the one that contains the suffix and an epenthetic vowel rather than the one containing the root vowel, so we get: fal-m > fəlam 'find you'.' Pearce 2006 p.266: 'The morphology of these words does not affect the choice of allophone.' (Foot heads are assigned by left-to-right quantity-sensitive iambic parsing over the whole word, prefixes included, cf. ACAL 2007 ex.(9) /K-paka-w/…
morph.elicq: Thesis section 2.2.1 (p.33): 'The following graphs give results from a measurement of 55 words collected from a folk story which I claim have the structure /CVCV/.' Section 2.2.1.2 (p.44): 'Because these forms are rare in natural speech, the only way to measure these consistently is to ask a speaker to produce several of these forms in a controlled setting. This was done, and careful measurements were taken of one speaker... Over 50 words with multiple suffixes were measured for amplitude, vowel quality, duration and tone'. Ch.4 fn.2: 'These pitch tracks show the words recorded in isolation to emphasize the contrast, but they were also measured in tone frames with similar results.'…
morph.stmt: Kera inflection is suffixing/enclitic: 'Verb suffixes denote the aspect, mood or object (direct or indirect). Similar suffixes denote a possessive when added to inalienable nouns' and 'The most common noun phrase affix is the definite article -ŋ... best analysed as a clitic', with 'Between 1 and 4 suffixes' stacking on the verb (mirk-t-n-m 'greeted you repeatedly'); the only prefixes are the non-productive gender/plural K-/T- (plural circumfixal k-...-w/-aŋ) and a frozen a-, while subject pronouns, negation (bà), question (mó), imperative (lá) and 'many tenses, aspects and moods' are separate words (Pearce 2007: 22-25).

tn.quote: Like all Chadic languages, Kera is tonal (Schuh 2003); its tonal system is comprised of the underlying tones /H/, /M/ and /L/. … In monosyllabic and disyllabic words, each syllable has a tone, regardless of the foot structure or syllable weight. This leads us to conclude that the tone-bearing unit is the syllable. … We should also note that there are no contour tones in Kera, so when two tones arrive on one syllable, one of them is deleted. … So far we have established that there are three phonemic tones in Kera, and that the VOT of the onset is progressively smaller as the tone is lower.
tn.cite: Pearce, Mary (2006). The interaction between metrical structure and tone in Kera. Phonology 23(2): 259-286. Cambridge University Press. doi:10.1017/S095267570600090X
tn.note: Three level tones H, M, L (enhanced by VOT), no contour tones; TBU is the syllable in short words, the foot head in longer ones; nouns show seven melodies (H M L LH HL MH HM); no word stress.

673.quote: The phonological word (PW) in Ketengban is the domain of one stress. The stressed syllable is frequently, but not always, accompanied by higher pitch than the non-stressed syllables. The majority of PWs consist of one to three syllables although words of up to five syllables are known to occur. 1.1 Stress. Stress is phonemic, as evidenced by the following contrasts: Between nouns: /'bume/ ['bumɛ] 'horsefly' /bu'me/ [bu'mɛ] 'short' /'kalum/ ['kalum] 'charcoal' /ka'lum/ [ka'lum] 'tapioca type' Between noun and verb: /'bana/ ['bana] 'to walk' /ba'na/ [ba'na] 'jaw' /'galuna/ ['galuna] 'vegetable …

674.dq: Disregarding levels above the phonemic word, a primary stress occurs on the first syllable of any noun stem of less than four syllables and on the second syllable of any stem over four. (1978:18 = 1971:13); the foot/phrase level is treated separately: 'The phonological foot ... is a unit of stress placement ... Feet are bounded by pause or by plus juncture' (1978:29).
674.dloc: Franklin & Franklin 1978: p.28 sec. 2.1.2.3 (Stress), p.18 (noun-stem stress = Franklin 1971:13 sec. 2.31), p.29 sec. 2.2.1 (phonological foot)
674.heavy: No weight criterion for primary stress. Only a non-primary 'minor stress' is produced on otherwise unstressed syllables by (1) high tone, (2) fortis consonants, (3) the geminate vowel /aa/ (1978:28); long vowels other than /aa/ are restricted to monosyllabic rhythm units (1971:12).
674.dflt: initial (no heavy category exists for primary stress)
674.prule: Non-phonemic stress: first syllable of words (nouns, pronouns, adjectives, time words); noun stems of more than four syllables stress the second syllable; verbs: stress position set by tone class and affixation (Class I unaffixed roots initial, affixed -> final stem syllable; other class second stem syllable). Language has phonemic (lexical) tone; stressed low tone is heard as mid.
674.srule: Non-primary 'minor stress' on otherwise unstressed syllables that carry high tone, a fortis consonant, or /aa/; no positional or rhythmic secondary stress is described (Kewa I [East Kewa] in Franklin & Franklin 1978:28). [Later, for East Kewa: Yarapea 2006:29-30 places a secondary stress on the penultimate syllable of words of more than five syllables.]

674.exq_: except verbs where it may occur elsewhere ... Affixation of tone Class I verbs causes stress to shift to final stem syllable (p.28); on the second syllable of any [noun] stem over four (p.18); suffix '-re, which is always stressed (p.32); na- 'negative' the prefix receives the stress (p.39)
674.tone: Phonemic tone (high vs low, acute = high; tone classes with perturbation rules: Kewa I sec. 2.1.2.1 Tone Classes I-III, sec. 2.3 noun and verb Classes I-IV); verb stress position depends on the stem's tone class (pp.28, 38-39); a stressed basic low tone is heard as mid (p.18); high tone on an unstressed syllable produces a minor stress (p.28). Dictionary entries are written without tone (p.19).

morph.rootq: §2.31 p.13: 'The perceptual or auditory height of a tone may be conditioned by stress placement (cf. Kewa I:35). Disregarding levels above the phonemic word, a primary stress occurs on the first syllable of any noun stem of less than four syllables and on the second syllable of any stem over four. Any basic low tone which occurs on such stressed syllables will be heard as mid.' (Verified verbatim on PDF p.23 by the adjudicator. Also §2.2 p.12: 'any rhythm unit (or phonological foot) is a unit of stress placement, each foot having an obligatory stress which is the nucleus (Kewa II:84)'; §2.6…
morph.elicq: Franklin 1971 gives no elicitation method for the stress statement itself (§2.31 p.13 simply asserts it, citing Kewa I:35). What is stated: tone patterns of verb stems 'are illustrated in the following frame ... The isolating frame consists of ní -wa "I [verb]-(1sg Pa)"' (§2.3 p.13); 'the basic tones of any stem can only be positively identified in an environment other than pre- or post-silence' (§2.31 p.14); and the grammar's primary material is 'a concordance of over 14,000 words of text in West Kewa' (§1.0 p.1). The East Kewa precursor (Kewa I, reprinted in PL C-53 p.29) says of stress: 'Thus far stress placement has only been determined for short constructions. No phonological…
morph.stmt: Kewa is suffixing: the verb is 'The verb base plus the obligatory Terminal or Non-Terminal suffix' (§3.21 p.38) with the formula v -> (NEG) + NUC + PHERI + (ASp3) + (CON/MOD) (§3.24 p.47), where the only pre-posed elements are the pre-clitics na- 'negative' and ma- 'causative' ('na- is a pre-clitic rather than a prefix', p.47); person-number-tense, imperative, aspect, benefaction and switch-reference are all suffixes, and nouns take no affixes of their own ('There are also no clitics or suffixes which occur solely with nouns', §3.25 p.52) but host case-like and word-level enclitics (-me, -para, -na, -re, -si, -nu, -lu).

675.dq: The Kiriwinan word consists of groups of syllables (see 2.2), one of which is given a certain prominence over the other syllables grouped with it. This prominence or stress is the phonetic feature which makes a word isolable from another word, as each phonological word may carry only one syllable with major stress. (2.3.1, p.41); cf. p.44 'Pitch, then, is not significant at the level of the phono…

675.heavy: a word-final CVm syllable (m is the only permitted coda) or a word-final syllable with a diphthongal nucleus (ai, au, ei, eu, oi, ou); weight is consulted only in the final syllable
675.dflt: penultimate (SR3); antepenultimate under SR2's shape-plus-no-morpheme-boundary condition
675.prule: Ordered rules on the phonological word: SR1 final stress if the final syllable is CVm or has a diphthongal nucleus; SR2 antepenultimate stress for words ending CVCi(C)a#, CVCu(C)a#, CVkala# or CVkana# with no morpheme boundary in the last three syllables; SR3 otherwise regular penultimate stress (about 95% of words). Emphatic speech may move final/penultimate stress back one syllable; some object-focus verb forms shift stress.
675.srule: Any word with two or more syllables before the main stress carries secondary stress(es). No regular phonetic principle: secondary stress picks out morphemes (morpheme-initial syllables) and reduplicative elements within the word, and, where morphemic structure permits, prefers two unstressed syllables between itself and the next stress (i.e. the third syllable back from the primary); a devoiced vowel between voiceless consonants passes the secondary to the preceding syllable; verb-focus reduplications may bear secondary stress on the syllable immediately before the primary.

morph.rootq: "Regular stress in Kiriwinan is on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word. About 95% of words follow this as the regular pattern. However, there are special circumstances to be found which place the stress in some cases on the final syllable and in other cases on the antepenultimate syllable of the word." (2.3.4, p.44). The only morphological reference is a morpheme-BOUNDARY condition on antepenultimate stress (SR2), not a root/stem domain: "The conditioning factor is the presence or absence of morpheme boundaries within the last three syllables of words having the specified phonetic shape. Where there is no boundary the stress placement is antepenultimate. If any of these words…
morph.elicq: "I studied the points of phonetic prominence in phonological words initially by listening and marking wherever such points of prominence occurred, which was easy. But it is not easy to state conclusively just what that prominence is. Therefore I supported my aural response to stress by using sonagrams to study the duration of syllables, and mingograph readings to give an indication of pitch and intensity. The sonagrams of slow speech were manifestly easier to follow than those of fast speech" (fn.27, p.43); the instrumental sample is a recorded text: "There are 61 phonological words in the segment Pesiana [App.1, Sequence 2, a slow explanatory monologue]. Stress is marked on them in…
morph.stmt: "Kiriwinan morphology is highly synthetic and has also some agglutinative features... In general the pattern of affixation in Kiriwinan shows an equal proportion of prefixes and suffixes. There are also some discontinuous morphemes, as for example the deictic: ma-tau-na 'that human'" (1.4, p.8); verb-word template R11: "Vb -> (comp) + subj + Vs + (obj) + (pl) [+ (emph)]" (3.5, p.67), i.e. TAM/realis and subject person are prefixed, object person, number, dative -ki and emphatic are suffixed; derivation (causative/instrumental 'verbal referents', verbaliser mila-/kabi-, nominaliser to-, classifiers on numerals/adjectives/deictics) is prefixal, inalienable possession suffixal.

675.sec_quote: Any word with two or more syllables before the stressed syllable features other points of prominence, which are referred to as secondary stress. There is no regular phonetic principle manifested in secondary stress patterns. ... wherever the morphemic structure permits ... the pattern of secondary stress prefers a space of two unstressed syllables between itself and the next stressed syllable.

evidence_works.detail: The paper restates the grammars' pattern (final heavy syllable stressed, otherwise the penult) and states the exact condition for antepenultimate stress: a high-vowel penult before a final [a], with no retraction when the penult has a non-high vowel or the ultima a high vowel, analysed as feet avoiding [a e o] in the unstressed syllable. This sharpens the catalog's Lawton-based entry, which gives the antepenultimate cases as 'in part determined phonetically'; the data are the same two sources, so it adds analysis, not new evidence.

677.dq: main stress falls on the last syllable containing a long vowel. If there is no long vowel main stress falls on the penultimate syllable if it is heavy and on the antepenultimate syllable if the penultimate syllable is light (StressTyp2 passage 1198 after Hayes 1995:279-281; StressTyp2 in_toto: 'In words of all sizes, primary stress falls on the right-most superheavy syllable ...')

677.heavy: Three-way scale: syllables with a long vowel (CVV(C), 'superheavy' in StressTyp2/Heinz terms) attract primary stress anywhere in the word (rightmost wins); closed syllables with a short vowel (CVC, 'heavy') count only in the right-edge default (closed penult beats antepenult) and for secondary stress; CV light.

677.prule: Primary stress on the rightmost long vowel of the word; if the word has no long vowel, on the penult if it is closed, otherwise on the antepenult if there is one, otherwise (disyllables) on the penult.

678.prule: Kimball 1991/1994: three pitch accents (low, high, high rising-falling); verbal accents morphologically motivated; in nouns accent is 'lexical in nature', every noun has one accented syllable, and 'the vast majority of root (i.e., underived) nouns' are regular: accent on the penult if it has a long vowel, otherwise on the ultima; 'the vast majority can be derived by rule'. Gordon, Martin & Langley 2015 (instrumental, c. 2,000 recorded words): the noun-final high pitch is a phrase-final intonational melody, not lexical; only a small class of underived nouns, plus nominalizations, loans and some compounds, carry lexical rising tone on the penult; verbs carry grammatical (grade) tone on the stem penult; stress proper (duration/intensity, explicitly distinct from tone accent) makes the first syllable of the word most prominent, with heavy (CVV, CVC) syllables, stem-final syllables and the first of two consecutive light syllables also prominent -- a left-to-right trochaic parse they call tentative.
678.srule: Gordon, Martin & Langley 2015: 114 (sec. 5.3; 'tentative', impressionistic): besides the most-prominent first syllable, 'heavy syllables (CVC and CVV), stem-final syllables, and the first in a sequence of two consecutive light syllables sound prominent', read as a left-to-right trochaic(ˈtika) 'rope', (ˈwaː)(ˈkasi) 'calf', (ˈok)(ˈʧos)(ˈbani) 'type of turtle'; not called secondary stress, no ranking among non-initial prominences. Revised by Gordon & Martin 2023: 283, 288: 'There is no phonetic evidence for rhythmic prominence in Koasati. However, heavy syllables (CVC and CVV) also are prominent' -- the trochaic/first-of-two-lights claim is dropped, heavy-syllable prominence kept. Gordon, Martin & Langley 2015 (ICPhS) treat the stem penult and heavy syllables (long V or sonorant coda) as docking sites of predictable pitch accents. Kimball 1991/1994: secondary accent not mentioned (one accent per noun).

678.tone: Gordon, Martin & Langley 2015 separate three things: phrase-final intonational melodies on nouns (final H, HL or L, 'phrase-final rather than lexical'), lexical rising tone on the penult of a small class of underived nouns (okwǒːɬi 'blueberry' vs okwaːla 'toad') plus nominalizations, some loans and noun+verb compounds, and grammatical grade tone (low or rising) on the penult of verb stems, with high pitch on the stem-final vowel; word stress (initial, duration/intensity) is 'distinct from the lexical tone accent'. Kimball 1994 instead describes three pitch accents (low, high, high rising-falling), morphologically motivated in verbs and lexical in nouns (penult if long vowel, else ultima).

morph.stmt: Martin 2025: 381: 'Verbs in Koasati are highly synthetic, with nine prefix slots, fifteen suffix slots, and different grades and internal changes to stems (Kimball 1991)'; p. 369: 'Person markers are prefixed in the patient and dative series. In the agent series, the first person singular -li (or -l) is always a suffix. The other agent person markers may be prefixed, infixed, or suffixed depending on verb class... Second, tone is used morphologically to convey aspectual…

tones: rising pitch/tone (lexical accent on penult of some nouns; g-grade)
tn.quote: 5. Prosody. Koasati displays a complex prosodic system featuring intonation, lexical and grammatical tone, and predictable stress. ... These different melodies are phrase-final rather than lexical. ... Nouns may also have lexical tonal accent, however. A small number of underived nouns have rising pitch on the penult. ... the l-grade ... is signaled by assigning low tone to the penult ... The g-grade expresses resulting states and is signaled by assigning a rising pitch to the penult ... Both of these grade patterns also have high pitch on the stem-final vowel

corr.words: Lexical tone is associated with certain nouns and is phonetically realized as a low-high (LH) rise that starts at the beginning of the syllable and reaches its high target late in the syllable or early in the next syllable ... The G-grade parallels lexical tone in nouns in consisting of a LHµ sequence realized on the stem penultimate syllable ... consistent with a Lµ+H analysis.

678.cfw: Kimball's grammar (1991) and dictionary (1994) describe a right-edge pitch accent on nouns (penult if it has a long vowel, otherwise the final syllable), while the instrumental studies of Gordon, Martin and Langley (2015) and Gordon and Martin (2023) find the first syllable most prominent, treat the final high pitch as phrase-level intonation, call Kimball's accent system "quite different from what we hear" and label their own stress analysis tentative, so two authoritative first-hand descriptions disagree on both placement and type of system with no third source to decide.

corr.detail: StressTyp2 entry: "Yazva: primary stress on the left-most heavy syllable, else on the final syllable; no secondary stress". The source gives: Stress the syllable containing the first (leftmost) 'heavy' vowel; if the word has only 'light' vowels, stress the final syllable (Itkonen 1955:29). Heavy = non-high vowels (a, o, ȯ, e and other reflexes of PPerm. non-high vowels), light = reflexes of PPerm. high u, i̮, i; in practice stress is mostly initial and moves right only when the first syllable has a high (least sonorous) vowel; Lytkin (via Normanskaja): first-syllable ɵ always passes stress to the next syllable, and surface high u, u̇, i are heavy or light word by word (etymologically).…

679.dq: Der Akzent ist gewöhnlich in der Silbe zu finden, die den ersten «schweren» Vokal hat. Gibt es nur «leichte» Vokale im Worte, so ist das Wort endbetont.
679.dloc: Itkonen 1955 pp. 28-29 (journal pagination; p. 29 saved); Normanskaja 2018 p. 6 and pp. 175-176 (citing Lytkin 1961: 33-34); Hayes 1995: 297 (StressTyp2 entry, carried)
679.heavy: Vowel aperture/height, not quantity or closure. Itkonen 1955:28-29: 'die Betonung hängt vom Öffnungsgrade der Vokale ab'; the reflexes of Proto-Permic high u, i̮, i are «leicht», all other (non-high) vowels «schwer»; a first-syllable 'minder sonorer, mit höchster Zungenstellung gebildeter Vokal' sends stress rightward; Itkonen likens schwer/leicht to Cheremis full vs reduced vowels 'nur vom Standpunkte der Betonung aus'. Lytkin 1961:33-34 (via Normanskaja 2018:175): non-narrow a, o, ȯ, e in the first syllable always stressed; first-syllable ɵ always throws stress to the next syllable; narrow u, u̇, i may be stressed or unstressed in polysyllables, attracting stress where other Komi dialects have non-high o, e̬, e and repelling it where they have high u, i (etymological, i.e. lexical on the surface). Hayes 1995:297 (carried): 'all non-high vowels pattern as heavy, while most high vowels are treated as light in some instances and heavy in others'.
679.dflt: final syllable, stated in the database-cited source: Itkonen 1955:29 'Gibt es nur «leichte» Vokale im Worte, so ist das Wort endbetont' (examples juka·śne, buzgine·, pe̮čkiśa·ń); = Hayes 1995:297 'otherwise the rightmost syllable' (carried). Lytkin as restated by Normanskaja adds only that first-syllable ɵ passes stress to the following syllable.
679.prule: Stress the syllable containing the first (leftmost) 'heavy' vowel; if the word has only 'light' vowels, stress the final syllable (Itkonen 1955:29). Heavy = non-high vowels (a, o, ȯ, e and other reflexes of PPerm. non-high vowels), light = reflexes of PPerm. high u, i̮, i; in practice stress is mostly initial and moves right only when the first syllable has a high (least sonorous) vowel; Lytkin (via Normanskaja): first-syllable ɵ always passes stress to the next syllable, and surface high u, u̇, i are heavy or light word by word (etymologically).
679.srule: Not mentioned in Itkonen 1955, pp. 28-30 (Permic section; his only Nebenakzent remark there concerns Udmurt). StressTyp2 codes secondary stress 'Absent' for lect Yazva; Lytkin 1970: 248-250, Rédei 1988: 116/370, Estill 2006 and Normanskaja 2018: 175-176 are likewise silent.

679.idn: Itkonen's rule (stress on the syllable with the first 'heavy' = non-high vowel, else on the final syllable) is stated for 'Ostpermjakisch', i.e. East Permyak = Komi-Yazva (his Russian résumé p. 33: 'в восточно-пермяцком или коми-язьвинском языке'; Glottolog komi1277, a separate language; = StressTyp2 lect 'Yazva'…

Auch heute liegt der Akzent meistens auf der ersten Silbe und verschiebt sich nur in dem Falle auf eine andere, wenn in der ersten Silbe ein minder sonorer, mit höchster Zungenstellung gebildeter Vokal ist.

morph.stmt: Exclusively suffixing and agglutinative: Wiedemann 1884 §19 p.45 derives words 'durch Ableitungssuffixe, welche an Zusammensetzungen so gut wie an einfache Wörter gehängt werden können', §84 p.115 'Stamm der Declination ist zugleich der Nominativ... und die Casus des Plurals sind denen des Singulars vollkommen gleich, nur dass der Stamm mit dem Pluralsuffix... verlängert ist', §96 the plural suffix 'nimmt... immer unverändert seine Stelle vor allen anderen Suffixen ein'; the only pre-root grammatical material is non-affixal - the person-inflected negative auxiliary og/on/oz standing proclitically before the connegative verb (§130, §17.4), the jussive particle med (§128), superlative…

679.sec_quote: Im anderen Zweige des Permischen, im Wotjakischen, sind die Wörter endbetont, wobei manchmal auch ein Nebenakzent in der ersten Silbe erscheint, z. B. ko.rkajosmy 'unsere Zimmer'.

679.cfw: Itkonen 1955 and Lytkin 1970 agree that in Komi-Yazva stress falls on the first syllable with a non-high vowel and on the last syllable when every vowel is high, but that is the Yazva lect (listed by Glottolog as a separate language), and Lytkin 1970 describes Komi-Zyrian proper as having free stress with only a tendency toward the first syllable, so the rule is secure for Yazva and does not describe Komi-Zyrian as a whole.

corr.detail: StressTyp2 entry: "Komi-Permyak: primary stress on the left-most heavy syllable, else on the final syllable; no secondary stress". The source gives: Stress is morphologized ('морфологизировано'): its place depends on the morpheme - some morphemes are unstressed (e.g. adjectival derivational -öсь, -тöм), some always stressed (verbal derivational -öт-, -ав-), some pull stress onto themselves or the preceding syllable; place of stress is also distinctive (góretni 'cry out' vs gorétni 'shout', ólan 'you live' vs olán 'life'; бы́дтас 'will bring up' vs быдта́с 'foster-child'). — StressTyp2 codes Komi-Permyak [koi] as F/L 'left-most heavy syllable, else final' with heavy = long vowels…

ev.text: 2.1.2. Ударение К-п.я. среди других пермских и финно-угорских языков занимает особое место - оно морфологизировано; наряду с этим является и фонологическим средством: местом ударения различаются не только значения слов и их оттенки (góretni ‘вскрикнуть’ и gorétni ‘крикнуть’, ólan ‘живёшь’ и olán ‘жизнь’). ... [5.7.0, южное наречие:] Наречие характеризуется отсутствием /l/, разноместным характером ударения (за исключением нижнеиньвенского диалекта), его фонологизацией и т. д. ... [северное наречие:] процессы морфологизации ударения и возникновения системы внешнеместных падежей находятся в развитии. ... Коми-язьвинское наречие по многим чертам близко примыкает к оньковскому и нижнеиньвенскому…

qtr.text: 2.1.2. The stress of the K[omi]-P[ermyak] language occupies a special place among the other Permic and Finno-Ugric languages - it is morphologized; alongside this it is also a phonological means: by the place of stress not only the meanings of words and their nuances are distinguished (góretni ‘to cry out’ and gorétni ‘to shout’, ólan ‘you live’ and olán ‘life’). ... [5.7.0, southern dialect group:] The dialect group is characterized by the absence of /l/, by the free (variable-position) character of the stress (with the exception of the Lower In'va dialect), by its phonologization, etc. ... …

680.dqtr: Translation of the quoted passage: Content words and function words are distinguished by stress: on the former falls the main stress, on the latter a secondary, additional one (cf. öш̀ын в΄ылын ‘on the window’, кер̀öс с΄айын ‘behind the mountain’), but more often they [the function words] are unstressed. (Batalova 1993 §2.2.2, final sentence; together with word-internal minimal pairs góretni/goré…
680.dq: Знаменательные и служебные слова различаются по ударению: на первые падает основное ударение, на вторые - побочное, дополнительное (ср. öш̀ын в΄ылын ‘на окне’, кер̀öс с΄айын ‘за горой’), но чаще они безударны. (Batalova 1993 §2.2.2, final sentence; together with word-internal minimal pairs góretni/gorétni, ólan/olán in §2.1.2)
680.dloc: §2.2.2 (morphonology; final sentence: content vs function words) and §2.1.2 (stress; minimal pairs); HTML, no page numbers (print pp. 229-239 per the page header)
680.heavy: Nothing is counted as heavy for Komi-Permyak proper: stress is morphologized (morpheme classes stressed/unstressed/stress-shifting). Only for the Komi-Yazva, On'kovo and Lower-Inva dialects does Batalova name a 'качественно-вокальная система ударения' (a vowel-QUALITY-based stress system), i.e. the 'heavy vowel' of Hayes 1980:58 / StressTyp2 is a vowel-quality class, not vowel length as the ST1 note ('long vowels') has it.
680.dflt: n/a for Komi-Permyak proper; in the dialectal vowel-quality system as carried by StressTyp2 from Hayes 1980:58: 'on the final vowel in words without heavy vowels'
680.prule: Stress is morphologized ('морфологизировано'): its place depends on the morpheme - some morphemes are unstressed (e.g. adjectival derivational -öсь, -тöм), some always stressed (verbal derivational -öт-, -ав-), some pull stress onto themselves or the preceding syllable; place of stress is also distinctive (góretni 'cry out' vs gorétni 'shout', ólan 'you live' vs olán 'life'; бы́дтас 'will bring up' vs быдта́с 'foster-child').
680.srule: Word-internal secondary stress: not mentioned in Batalova 1993 (§2.1.2 stress, p. 230; §2.2.2, p. 231; §2.7.0 dialects, pp. 238-239, all read). The only secondary ('побочное, дополнительное') stress she mentions is phrase-level: a function word/postposition after a content word carries a weaker stress or, more often, none (öшын вы́лын 'на окне').

morph.rootq: KG sketch, 'УДАРЕНИЕ' (verified): «Место ударения в коми-пермяцком языке чаще зависит от морфемы: одни морфемы безударные, другие ударные, третьи перетягивают ударения на себя или на предшествующий слог. Такой тип ударения принято называть морфологизированным. Безударными обычно являются словообразовательные суффиксы прилагательных: са́-öсь 'запачканный сажей' (са 'сажа'), бу́с-öсь 'пыльный', ки́-тöм 'безрукий', ко́к-тöм 'безногий'. Всегда ударные словообразовательные суффиксы глаголов, например: мич-ö́т-ны 'окрасить' (мич 'краса'), шоч-а́в-ны 'редеть'... Присоединение некоторых суффиксов вызывает перемещение ударения: ко́книт 'лёгкий', кокни́т-ик 'лёгонький', ми́ян 'наш'…
morph.elicq: No statement of method or evidence type in any of the three sources; stress facts are presented only as isolated citation-form minimal pairs, e.g. KG sketch: «Коми-пермяцкое ударение может служить средством разграничения частей речи, а внутри одной и той же части речи – средством различения форм слов, например: бы́дтас 'воспитает' (от быдтыны 'воспитать') и быдта́с 'воспитанник'; ма́втас 'смажет' и мавта́с 'мазь'; о́лан 'живёшь' и ола́н 'жизнь'; сё́ян 'ешь' и сёя́н 'еда'; гö́рись 'пашущий' и гöри́сь 'пахарь'»; the only phrase-level datum is Batalova §2.2.2 «öш̀ын в΄ылын 'на окне', кер̀öс с΄айын 'за горой'» (noun + postposition).
morph.stmt: Almost exclusively suffixing and agglutinative: «В коми-пермяцком языке очень продуктивна суффиксация; префиксация не характерна. В формообразовании используется единственная приставка мед-» (ИЯз РАН sketch); «Слово в коми-пермяцком языке состоит из следующих морфем: корень, суффиксы словообразования, суффиксы словоизменения (удж-ал-ісь-ным-лöн 'у [нашего] работника')... Префиксов в коми-пермяцком языке немного. К ним относятся лишь мед- со значением 'самый, наи-' и не- (заимствованный из русского языка)» (KG sketch); «Морфологический тип К.-п. я. агглютинативный с выраженными чертами флективности» (Batalova 1993 §2.3.0); verbal negation is the one systematically pre-posed grammatical…

The source gives: Stress on the first high-toned syllable of the word; in all-low-toned words on the first syllable. 681.dq: In Wurzeln liegt er auf der ersten hochtonigen Silbe; in rein tieftonigen Wurzeln auf der ersten Silbe ... Bei affigierten Wörtern gilt die genannte Regel jedoch nicht ... Da der Druckakzent nicht generell auf die erste hochtonige Silbe eines Wortes fällt, kann der Druckakzent auch funktional distinktiv sein.
681.dloc: Reh 1985, Kap. 2 Phonologie, §2.4 Prosodologie, §2.4.2 'Druckakzent', pp. 78-79 (Google Books view, vol. GIQOAAAAYAAJ; held)
681.heavy: High tone: stress goes to the first high-toned syllable (StressTyp2 ST1 note ': high tone'); in affixed words vowel length in the first root syllable is listed as a fourth co-determinant alongside affix tones, root tones and root syllable count. No statement that closed syllables or long vowels per se attract stress in simplex words.
681.dflt: first syllable of the root in all-low-toned roots (Reh states the default for roots; in affixed words placement follows her affix rules: a high-toned case prefix takes the stress if the first root vowel is short, otherwise stress stays root-initial)
681.prule: In roots, stress on the first high-toned syllable; in all-low-toned roots on the first syllable (ˈtárì, sàˈrí, àsàˈní, ˈàlàkà, ˈkùsòròntìŋ). Reh: this rule does not hold in affixed words, where placement depends on the affix's tone, the root's tones, the root's syllable count and the vowel length of the first root syllable; a high-toned case prefix (kí-, nkí-, án-, má-, yá-) takes the stress if the noun is monosyllabic, all-low with a short first vowel, or disyllabic LH (ˈkú-lú, ˈki-mìsì, ˈa-sari), otherwise stress 'in der Regel' stays on the root (ki-ˈsálân, kí-ˈmèetèn). Stress 'does not generally fall on the first high-toned syllable of a word' and can be distinctive alone: íˈdína 'he lifts up' vs ˈídína 'he lifts up repeatedly', tonally identical. Reh flags stress as not yet investigated in detail ('muß noch detailliert untersucht werden').
681.srule: When one of the high-toned case prefixes (kí-, nkí-, án-, má-, yá-) is attached and the first high tone of the root lies on the third or fourth root syllable, that prefix receives a secondary stress (Nebendruckakzent), the main stress staying on the root; no other secondary or rhythmic stress is described (Reh 1985: 78-79, who adds that stress 'muß noch detailliert untersucht werden').
681.quote: Das Verhalten des Druckakzents muß noch detailliert untersucht werden. In Wurzeln liegt er auf der ersten hochtonigen Silbe; in rein tieftonigen Wurzeln auf der ersten Silbe … Bei affigierten Wörtern gilt die genannte Regel jedoch nicht … Die Position des Druckakzents wird bei affigierten Wörtern durch mehrere Faktoren bestimmt, und zwar durch (1) das Tonmuster des Affixes, (2) die Tonstruktur der Wurzel und (3) die Silbenzahl der Wurzel, sowie (4) durch die Vokallänge der ersten Wurzelsilbe. … (b) In allen anderen Fällen bleibt der Druckakzent in der Regel unverändert auf der jeweiligen Wurz…
681.loc: Reh 1985, Kap. 2 Phonologie, §2.4 Prosodologie, §2.4.2 'Druckakzent' (ends at the heading '2.5 Silbenstruktur und Silbenfolge'), p. 78 with the adjacent pages (the running heads '78 2 Phonologie' and '2.4 Prosodologie 79' fall inside the passage; StressTyp2 cites p. 78); read in Google Books view, vol. GIQOAAAAYAAJ (openly shown excerpt excerpts, chained word for word)
681.idn: Krongo, autonym nìinò mó-dì ('Sprache von Zuhause'), a member of the Kadugli group, spoken chiefly in Tabanya, Toroji and Angolo (Nuba Mountains); Reh's data come mainly from Tabanya (Hall & Hall 2004:65 call her variety 'Krongo-Tabanya').; data: Nuba Mountains, Sudan: reconnaissance visit March 1980; fieldwork in…
681.exq_: Bei affigierten Wörtern gilt die genannte Regel jedoch nicht ... In allen anderen Fällen bleibt der Druckakzent in der Regel unverändert auf der jeweiligen Wurzelsilbe. ... Imperfektiv: (a) í'dína 'er hebt (gleich) hoch' (b) 'ídína 'er hebt wiederholt hoch'
681.tone: Tone language: two tonemes, high and low, distinctive lexically and grammatically (aspect 'Apotonie', derivation) (Reh 1985 §2.4.1.1, p. 75). Stress placement is stated separately (§2.4.2) and refers to tone: first high-toned syllable of the root, else root-initial.

tn.quote: Das Krongo besitzt zwei Toneme: hoch (H): und tief (T): ` . Der Ton ist auf lexikalischer und auf grammatischer Ebene distinktiv . Auf der grammatischen Ebene dient er der Aspektunterscheidung (Apotonie), der Derivation ... Bei den komplexen Tönen handelt es sich nicht um Toneme, sondern um Tonkombinationen . Fallende Töne entstehen zumeist dadurch, daß ein finaler tieftoniger Vokal nach einer hochtonigen Silbe mit langem Vokal schwindet, z.B. kanáây ... Steigton findet sich in dem Verb caáw ' gehen ' . Komplexe Töne kommen nur auf Silben mit langen Vokalen vor .
tn.translation: Krongo has two tonemes: high (H): [´] and low (T): `. Tone is distinctive at the lexical and at the grammatical level. At the grammatical level it serves to distinguish aspect (apotony), derivation ... The complex tones are not tonemes but tone combinations. Falling tones mostly arise when a final low-toned vowel is lost after a high-toned syllable with a long vowel, e.g. kanáây ... A rising tone is found in the verb caáw 'go'. Complex tones occur only on syllables with long vowels.

tn.note: Two tonemes H and L, lexically and grammatically distinctive (aspect, derivation); falling/rising tones are H+L combinations on long vowels only. Downstep in noun plurals. 682.heavy: No weight criterion for stress. Connell et al. 2000:13 define heavy syllables only for tone-contour licensing: 'in non-final syllables, pitch contours generally occur only in heavy syllables, i.e., in syllables having the shapes (C)VV (where VV represents either a long vowel or diphthong) or (C)VC.' 682.idn: Connell, Hayward & Ashkaba 2000 describe the Barka dialect of Kunama (title: 'Barka Dialect'), with Marda checked and found not to differ for the tonal phenomena examined; Barka (Glottolog bark1246) is a dialect of the record's language Kunama (kuna1268).
682.tone: Register tone language per Connell, Hayward & Ashkaba 2000: three level lexical tones (High, Mid, Low) that combine into contour tones, contours word-internally largely confined to heavy (C)VV/(C)VC syllables; tone also functions grammatically (e.g. number in possessive determiners, Low-toned dual -mme), and the authors find no contrastive lexical stress.

tn.quote: Kunama operates a register tone system in that its basic tones are level. There is no obvious down step of the sort that leads to terracing … Three significant contrasts in relatively level pitches are widely in evidence. We identify these as High (H), Mid (M) and Low (L) … In addition to these three level pitches, a number of contrastive pitch contours are also encountered on single syllables. In all, there are three falling contours and at least one rising contour. … it has seemed appropriate to represent these contours in the transcription as sequences of H, M, and L tones
tn.cite: Connell, Bruce A., Richard J. Hayward & John Abraha Ashkaba. 2000. Observations on Kunama Tone (Barka Dialect). Studies in African Linguistics 29(1): 1-41.
tn.locator: sec. 2.1 'Pitch phenomena', p. 3 and p. 8; analysis as level sequences sec. 2.2 p. 13; domain p. 20
tn.note: Three level tones, High, Mid and Low, counted by mora; falls (HM, ML, HL) and rises (MH) are level sequences; melodies belong to morphemes; floating tonal morphemes; no downstep; no lexical stress.

683.dq: primary stress falls on the only long vowel in the word or on the rightmost if there is more than one (5a); if there is no long vowel, primary stress falls on the initial syllable (5b).
683.dloc: McGarrity 2008 sec. 2.2 'Stress', pp.57-58 (citing Thompson 1976:217); sec. 3.1 pp.61-62; sec. 3.2 pp.63-64 (quoting Thompson 1988:6)
683.heavy: Syllables containing long vowels are heavy (underlyingly bimoraic); closed syllables and short-vowel syllables are light and do not attract stress ([káːwaj] 'south', [kúnpantin] 'flog'). McGarrity adds that an initial light open syllable bearing default primary stress is made heavy by geminating the following onset (/pama/ -> [pám.ma], Thompson 1988:6), i.e. CVC is contextually heavy word-initially but never attracts stress.
683.prule: Primary stress on the rightmost long vowel in the word; if the word has no long vowel, primary stress on the initial syllable (default-to-opposite-side).
683.srule: Secondary stress on every long vowel not bearing the primary and on the initial syllable when the primary is non-initial ([ʔìlpíːna] 'return', [pùːtáːwu] 'red bream', [ùntàːkúːpi] 'archer fish'); in words without long vowels Thompson also places a secondary on the second vowel ([pámà] 'Aboriginal person'), which McGarrity, following Hayes 1995:296, leaves unmarked. Thompson's own 1988 wording: secondary 'on the preceding long vowel, if any, otherwise on the first vowel of the word'; stress is 'predictable, but not rigid'.
683.quote: Stress assignment in this language is prominence-driven, based on syllable weight. As shown in (5) below, primary stress falls on the only long vowel in the word or on the rightmost if there is more than one (5a); if there is no long vowel, primary stress falls on the initial syllable (5b). Syllables containing long vowels are considered to be heavy for the purposes of stress assignment, as they are underlyingly bimoraic. According to Thompson, closed syllables and syllables containing short vowels are light and do not attract stress. (5) Kuuku-Yaʔu primary stress pattern a. Primary stress fa…
683.loc: McGarrity 2008 sec. 2.2 'Stress', pp.57-58 (citing Thompson 1976:217); sec. 3.1 pp.61-62; sec. 3.2 pp.63-64 (quoting Thompson 1988:6)
683.idn: Kuuku-Yaʔu (Kuuku Ya'u), Pama-Nyungan, Cape York, Australia; per Thompson 1988 the Kuuku Ya'u coastal dialect of the Lockhart River 'Sand Beach' language (North-Eastern Pama subgroup), spoken with Umpila by the few remaining older speakers at Lockhart River Aboriginal Community, Queensland; data: McGarrity: all data…
683.exq_: Kuuku Ya'u and Umpila have predictable, but not rigid, primary and secondary stress patterns. The stress is quite readily affected by emphasis, mood, fast speech etc., and frequently the effect is to equalise or reverse primary and secondary stress.

685.prule: As stated: primary stress on the first syllable of the word, unless the second or third syllable is long (long vowel), in which case that syllable is stressed; occasional word-final stress (da're:) called abnormal, attributed to contraction. The source's own transcriptions on the same pages also show unflagged 2nd/3rd-syllable stress on syllables with no marked length (mad'böröma, jila'mɛla, ŋa'gini, gwal'maruwa, gu'mununda, mi'labira, mi'juwura), mostly prefix + root shapes.
685.srule: In words of four or more syllables there is usually a secondary stress on alternate syllables after the primary, e.g. ['gwa:r̃a,bila] 'bandicoot', ['dwa:rim,bira] 'rat' (initial primary, secondary on the third syllable); no weight condition is stated for secondary stress.

686.dq: Words of two syllables are accented on the first syllable ... Words of more than two syllables are accented on the Penult if that is long ...; otherwise on the Antepenult
686.heavy: A syllable is 'long' (i) by nature if it contains a long vowel or diphthong, (ii) by position if it contains a short vowel followed by two consonants or a double consonant (x, z); a short vowel before mute + l/r is 'properly short' ('common', long only optionally in verse); h and the u of qu/gu/su do not count as consonants.

686.prule: Words of two syllables: accent on the first syllable. Words of more than two syllables: accent on the penult if it is long (by nature or by position), otherwise on the antepenult.
686.srule: Not mentioned in Allen & Greenough 1903 (secs. 11-12 'Quantity', 'Accent', pp. 6-7; Prosody secs. 602-612, pp. 401-410 read): one accent per word; the only other prominence discussed is the metrical ictus of verse. Hayes 1995: 91 sets Latin secondary stress aside 'since the data are not clearly established'.

morph.rootq: A&G sec. 12: 'Words of two syllables are accented on the first syllable: as, Rō'ma, fi'dēs, tan'gō. Words of more than two syllables are accented on the Penult if that is long (as, amī'cus, monē'tur, contin'git); otherwise on the Antepenult (as, do'minus, a'lacris, dissociā'bilis).' The rule is stated on syllable count and weight from the right word edge with no reference to root or stem; the only morphological provisos are sec. 12a 'When an enclitic is joined to a word, the accent falls on the syllable next before the enclitic, whether long or short: as, dea'que, amāre've, tibi'ne, ita'que' and Exc. 1 'Certain apparent compounds of faciō retain the accent of the simple verb: as…
morph.elicq: No evidential basis is given for the accent rule in sec. 12; the grammar describes a reconstructed classical pronunciation: sec. 8 'The so-called Roman Pronunciation of Latin aims to represent approximately the pronunciation of classical times.' (Dead language: the description rests on grammatical tradition, not on elicited words, frames, texts or measurements, and the book does not say so explicitly.)
morph.stmt: A&G sec. 21a: 'Inflectional changes sometimes take place in the body of a word, or at the beginning, but oftener in its termination'; sec. 24 'The body of a word, to which the terminations are attached, is called the stem' - i.e. all inflection (case/number, person, tense, mood, voice) and productive derivation (sec. 232 'Derived Stems are formed from roots or from other stems by means of suffixes') is suffixal, the only prefixal morphology being prepositional/inseparable preverbs and adjectival per-/sub-/in- (sec. 267 'Many syntactic compounds are formed by prefixing a Particle') plus perfect reduplication (sec. 177c).

tn.quote: Based on recent typological studies provided by phoneticians and phonologists, it is most likely that the Italic accent had a dominant stress nature in the period when vowel reduction (and deletion as its extreme form) occurred … languages with pitch accent may have accentual contrasts within a single syllable: for a heavy syllable, two kinds of prominence {rising/falling}, as seen in Ancient Greek, Lithuanian, and so forth. There seems to be no such phenomenon observable for Latin or Italic in general.
tn.cite: Nishimura, Kanehiro. 2014. On accent in the Italic languages: nature, position, and history. Studia Linguistica Universitatis Iagellonicae Cracoviensis 131: 161–192. doi:10.4467/20834624SL.14.009.2017
tn.locator: pp. 163–164, §1 'The Nature of Accent and Vowel Reduction / Deletion'
tn.note: No lexical tone: the Latin accent is argued to be mainly stress, with no rising/falling accent contrasts within a syllable; a Greek-style pitch accent in Literary Latin is reported as disputed.

686.cfw: 4 independent first-hand descriptions agree (2 state the same rule, 1 refine it); none contradicts.

evidence_works.detail: Latin is the article's textbook weight-sensitive example: penult if heavy, otherwise antepenult, modelled as a right-to-left transducer in which the penult is the only position where weight matters. This matches the catalog rule exactly.
